content: The earliest documented evidence of cancer originates from ancient Egyptian literature, specifically the Edwin Smith Papyrus, which dates back to approximately 3000 BC. This text describes eight cases of breast tumors treated with cauterization using a tool referred to as a fire drill. The document explicitly states that the disease was considered untreatable, as it notes, There is no treatment. In 1761, Giovanni Morgagni of Padua became the first to perform autopsies to establish a connection between illness and pathological findings. Scottish surgeon John Hunter (1728–1793) proposed that cancerous tumors could be surgically removed if they were localized and had not invaded surrounding tissues, describing such tumors as movable. During the 1700s, Hunter also hypothesized that tumors originated from lymphatic fluid continuously produced by the blood. In the 19th century, Rudolf Virchow was the first to link diseases, including cancer, to microscopic pathology, advancing the understanding of cellular abnormalities. Earlier, in the mid-17th century, Dutch physicians Zacutus Lusitani (1575–1642) and Nicholas Tulp (1593–1674) published observations suggesting that breast cancer might be contagious, based on cases involving multiple members of the same household. In 1713, Bernardino Ramazzini, an Italian physician, noted a higher prevalence of breast cancer among nuns, which he attributed to the absence of childbearing and hormonal influences, thus establishing an early link between hormones and breast cancer. In 1719, German surgeon Lorenz Heister described surgical techniques for mastectomy and lumpectomy in his book Chirurgie. In the late 19th century, William Stewart Halsted, a professor of surgery at Johns Hopkins University, introduced the radical mastectomy, a procedure that became a cornerstone of breast cancer treatment for decades. Around the same time, in 1896, Thomas Beatson, a graduate of the University of Edinburgh, discovered the relationship between oophorectomy (surgical removal of the ovaries) and breast cancer, laying the groundwork for hormonal therapy in breast cancer management. In the 20th century, significant advancements were made in breast cancer detection and treatment. Modern mammography techniques were developed in the late 1960s, and by 1976, the American Cancer Society officially recommended mammography as a screening tool. During the 1970s, clinical trials demonstrated that less extensive surgical procedures were as effective as radical surgeries for many women with breast cancer. By the final decades of the 20th century, surgical techniques evolved to minimize the removal of healthy tissue while excising tumors. In the 1990s, the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes were identified as being associated with an increased risk of developing breast cancer, marking a significant milestone in understanding the genetic basis of the disease. Additionally, in the late 1990s, trastuzumab (Herceptin), the first therapeutic monoclonal antibody for breast cancer, was approved, revolutionizing targeted therapy for HER2-positive breast cancer.
